state.case_summary:
A 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of severe occipital and temporal headaches that were paroxysmal, aggravated by changes in position, and associated with bilateral blurry vision and morning projectile vomiting. Neurological examination showed a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome with ataxia, imbalance, uncoordinated movements, bilateral nystagmus, and stage I bilateral papilledema. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no abnormalities. Brain MRI revealed an inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis measuring 40 × 31 × 29 mm, hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion filled the foramen of Magendie, exerted mass effect on the medulla, and showed no surrounding edema on FLAIR. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated increased signal, and GRE T2* sequences showed no hemorrhage or calcification. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed an elevated choline peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate signal.
